{{short description|Rate at which susceptible individuals acquire an infectious disease}}
In [[epidemiology]], '''force of infection''' (denoted <math>\lambda</math>) is the rate at which [[Susceptible individual|susceptible]] individuals acquire an [[infectious disease]].<ref name ="75years">{{cite journal |pmid= 19765352|year= 2010|last1= Hens|first1= N.|last2= Aerts|first2= M.|last3= Faes|first3= C.|last4= Shkedy|first4= Z.|last5= Lejeune|first5= O.|last6= Van Damme|first6= P.|last7= Beutels|first7= P.|title= Seventy-five years of estimating the force of infection from current status data|journal= Epidemiology and Infection|volume= 138|issue= 6|pages= 802–12|doi= 10.1017/S0950268809990781|hdl= 10067/791410151162165141|hdl-access= free}}</ref> Because it takes account of susceptibility it can be used to compare the rate of transmission between different [[Cohort (statistics)|groups]] of the [[Population (human biology)|population]] for the same infectious disease, or even between different infectious diseases. That is to say, <math>\lambda</math> is directly proportional to <math>\beta</math>; the effective [[Transmission (medicine)|transmission]] rate.

:<math>
\lambda = \frac {\mbox{number of new infections}} {\mbox{number of susceptible persons exposed} \times \mbox{average duration of exposure}}
</math>

Such a calculation is difficult because not all new infections are reported, and it is often difficult to know how many susceptibles were exposed. However, <math>\lambda</math> can be calculated for an infectious disease in an [[endemic (epidemiology)|endemic]] state if homogeneous mixing of the population and a rectangular population distribution (such as that generally found in developed countries), rather than a [[Population Pyramid|pyramid]], is assumed. In this case, <math>\lambda</math> is given by:

:<math>
\lambda = \frac {1} {A}
</math>

where <math>A</math> is the average age of infection. In other words, <math>A</math> is the average time spent in the susceptible group before becoming infected. The rate of becoming infected (<math>\lambda</math>) is therefore <math>1/A</math> (since rate is 1/time). The advantage of this method of calculating <math>\lambda</math> is that data on the average age of infection is very easily obtainable, even if not all cases of the disease are reported.{{cn|date=May 2023}}
